transcript.content: Hello, I'm Dr. [Your Name]. Can you tell me your name and what brings you in today?

Hi, doctor. My name is Julian. And, um, as for why I'm here today, it's... it's kind of a long story, to be honest. See, I work as a bookkeeping clerk, mostly doing accounting and auditing stuff, dealing with a ton of paperwork and data entry, which I've been doing since I got out of high school. Usually, I'm really good at it, very methodical, you know? But lately... lately I've started doing these things at work, and even at my night classes, that just... they really do not make any sense at all. Not even to me. 

Like, for example, the other day I had this massive stack of expense receipts to process. Normal stuff, travel expenses, office supplies, whatever. But instead of just entering them into the spreadsheet like I always do, I got out of my chair and found myself down on the carpet, just lining every single receipt up all across the floor, edge to edge, making this huge, perfect grid. I couldn't really tell you why I was doing it, it just felt like the only way to handle them in that moment. 

And then there's my calculator—I use a standard 10-key for the auditing—and I've been tapping the keys in these very specific patterns. I'll just sit there tapping the calculator in sets of nine. Exactly nine. Like, tap-tap-tap, tap-tap-tap, tap-tap-tap. Over and over. If I lose count or someone interrupts me, I have to clear it and start the nine taps all over again before I can even look at the numbers. It's so distracting. 

But I think the thing that really made me realize I needed to come in was what happened by the printer. I was supposed to be making copies of the quarterly reports, but I just ended up standing right next to the copier with both of my hands held up in the air. Just standing there, totally still, holding my hands up like that for I don't even know how long, until one of the managers finally walked by and stopped to ask if I was okay. And it's just... it's really starting to disrupt my job, and I just don't understand why I'm doing any of this.
Julian, when you find yourself doing these repetitive actions like lining up receipts or tapping the calculator keys, do you feel anxious or upset during or after doing them?

Well, that's the thing, doctor, and it's something I've spent a lot of time trying to figure out myself, honestly. Because you'd think, right? You'd think I'd be sitting there tapping the calculator or staring at the receipts on the floor and feeling this overwhelming sense of dread or panic, like I'm trying to ward off something terrible. But... I don't. Not really. 

It's more like... I'm just doing it. There's no big rush of anxiety that pushes me to do it, and there's no wave of relief after it's done. It's not like I'm sitting there thinking, "Oh God, if I don't tap these keys nine times, the whole audit is going to fail and I'll get fired." It's nothing like that. It's just... a compulsion, I guess? But without the emotional weight behind it. 

I mean, I *am* upset about the fact that it's happening, obviously, because it's completely messing up my workflow. Like, when my manager walked by while I was standing by the copier with my hands in the air, I felt incredibly embarrassed. Mortified, really. My face got all hot, and I had to stammer out some excuse about stretching my back, which I don't think he bought for a second. So, yes, the *consequences* of doing these things make me upset. I worry about my job performance, I worry about my coworkers thinking I'm losing my mind, I worry about falling behind in my night classes because I'm spending twenty minutes arranging my highlighters instead of reading the textbook. 

But the actual acts themselves? The tapping, the lining things up, the freezing in place? In the moment, it just feels like something my body has decided it needs to do, and my brain is just along for the ride, completely disconnected from any sort of fear or anxiety. It's almost... blank. Just a blank, mechanical need to complete the pattern. And that blankness, that lack of any real reason or feeling behind it, is almost more frustrating than if I *was* anxious, you know? At least if I was anxious, I could point to something and say, "That's why I'm doing this." But instead, I'm just left trying to explain to my supervisor why it took me an hour to process a stack of receipts that should have taken ten minutes, and I have absolutely nothing to tell him.
Julian, while you're doing these repetitive actions—like tapping the calculator or arranging receipts—do you have a sense that what you're doing might be unnecessary or excessive?

Well, yeah, absolutely. I mean, that's the whole crux of the problem, really. I know it's unnecessary. I know it's completely, utterly excessive. It's not like I'm sitting there thinking, "Ah, yes, tapping this calculator nine times is a vital step in the auditing process." I know it's not. I've been doing this job since I graduated high school, right? I know exactly how to process a travel expense report. You look at the date, the amount, the category, you type it into the cell, you move on. It takes maybe thirty seconds per receipt if you're being thorough. 

So when I'm down on my hands and knees in my cubicle, carefully aligning the edges of a receipt from a generic coffee shop with a receipt from a car rental place, making sure the gap between them is exactly the same as the gap between the next two... I am fully aware that it is a complete waste of time. I can almost hear my own brain saying, "Julian, what are you doing? This is ridiculous. You have a stack of fifty of these to get through by three o'clock and you've spent ten minutes on the first row of your little floor grid." 

And it's the same with the calculator. I know standard 10-key by touch, I don't even have to look at the keys usually. So when I stop in the middle of reconciling a column of figures to tap-tap-tap, tap-tap-tap, tap-tap-tap... I know I'm just delaying the work. I know it's excessive. But knowing that doesn't seem to stop it from happening. It's like... it's like there's a disconnect between my logical understanding of my job requirements and whatever part of my brain is currently driving my physical actions. 

I'll be standing there, like with the copier incident. I knew I was just supposed to hit 'start' and wait for the quarterly reports to print. I knew that holding my hands up in the air was doing absolutely nothing to facilitate the copying process. It wasn't fixing a paper jam, it wasn't loading toner, it was just... standing there like an idiot. And I knew it! I knew it the whole time I was doing it, which just makes the whole thing so incredibly frustrating. Because if I thought it was necessary, maybe I could justify it to myself, you know? But I know it's not. I know it's just bizarre, excessive behavior that's keeping me from doing the job I'm actually paid to do, and I just... I can't seem to bridge the gap between knowing it's pointless and actually stopping myself from doing it.

Julian, when you're doing these repetitive actions, like tapping the calculator or arranging receipts, is there a thought in your mind that something bad will happen if you don't finish them a certain way?

No, not at all. And that's exactly what makes it so confusing. There's no thought in my head telling me that something terrible is going to happen. It's not like I'm sitting there thinking, "If I don't tap this calculator exactly nine times, the office is going to catch on fire," or "If these receipts aren't perfectly aligned on the carpet, I'm going to get into a car crash on the way home." 

I've actually read about things like that, you know? Like where people think something catastrophic is going to happen if they don't flip a light switch a certain number of times. I saw a documentary about it once back in high school, and it sounded completely exhausting to live with that kind of fear. But for me, there is absolutely none of that. There's no impending sense of doom. No catastrophic thinking whatsoever. 

And honestly, doctor, that's the whole reason I made this appointment. Like I was saying when we first started talking, I came in because I have started doing all these things at work and at my night classes that just completely do not make sense. If I had a reason—even a crazy reason, like trying to prevent a disaster—at least it would be a reason! But instead, I'm just lining up endless rows of receipts across the floor, or I'm tapping that calculator in sets of nine over and over, or I'm just standing there frozen by the copier with my hands held up in the air until someone physically stops and asks if I am okay. 

There's no voice warning me of danger, no fear of bad consequences... just these completely senseless actions that I can't seem to explain to myself or anyone else. And when you're someone who is used to everything balancing out perfectly at the end of the day, like I am with my accounting work, dealing with something this illogical is just... it's really hard to wrap my head around.

Julian, when you're doing these repetitive actions, even though you don't feel anxious or fear something bad happening, do you feel that completing them in a certain way might somehow prevent something unpleasant or make things feel 'just right'?

Well, that’s a really interesting way to put it, doctor, "just right," because... I mean, in my line of work, everything is about making things exactly right. When I’m reconciling an account at the end of the month, and the debits equal the credits down to the absolute penny, *that* is a "just right" feeling. It’s satisfying, you know? It makes sense. It's logical. But these... these other actions? The tapping the calculator keys or arranging the receipts on the carpet? It’s not like that at all. Not even a little bit. 

I don't get any sense of completion or satisfaction from it. I don't step back and look at the grid of receipts and think, "Ah, perfect, everything is exactly how it should be." It's more like... I'm just stuck in a loop. And as for preventing something unpleasant? No, absolutely not. If anything, doing the actions is what *causes* the unpleasantness! Because, like I was saying before, I’m wasting so much time, I’m embarrassing myself in front of my manager at the copier, I’m falling behind on the reading for my night classes... 

So, no, there’s no relief, no feeling of perfection or things settling into place. It’s just this mechanical drive. It’s like a motor running without being connected to any gears. I just do it, and then eventually I stop, but not because it finally feels "right" or because I've achieved some goal. I don't even really know why I stop, to be honest. I just kind of... snap out of it, or someone interrupts me, like when my supervisor walked by. It’s incredibly frustrating because I'm a numbers guy. I like logic. I like things to have a clear purpose and a clear result. And this has absolutely zero purpose, zero payoff, zero "just right" feeling at the end of it. It's just an empty action, over and over, with no real resolution.
